newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Police say Dili legislature stoned, protest ends.
newsitem.headline: Police say Dili legislature stoned, protest ends.

text.p: East Timorese youths, angered by Indonesian attacks on Nobel Peace laureate Bishop Carlos Belo, stoned the territory's legislature in Dili on Wednesday but later dispersed peacefully, police reported.
"There were some windows broken, but not many," East Timor's deputy police chief Colonel Atok Rismanto told Reuters by telephone.

He said about four truck-loads of students were involved. He did not elaborate. There had also been an orderly march on the seafront outside the governor's office, but the crowd had started to disperse around noon (0500 GMT).
"There were no other incidents. The situation is under control. It is calm and normal again," Rismanto said. Other residents also said the protesters appeared to have dispersed.
Rismanto said no one had been detained.

The governor was out of the city for the day visiting rural areas in the territory, some 2,000 km (1,200 miles) east of Jakarta. Police said a middle-ranking official met the students at the office but there were no details.

Eyewitnesses said more than a thousand students and high school pupils had earlier gathered in front of the University of East Timor campus. The witnesses said police in riot gear had blocked off streets in the area.

The demonstrations appeared to have been sparked largely by strong criticism and protests in Jakarta against Belo, probably the most powerful and highly-regarded civilian in mainly Catholic East Timor.

Television footage seen in Dili on Tuesday night showed a demonstration in Jakarta by more than 2,000 members of youth groups allied to the country's ruling Golkar party who demanded the expulsion of Belo from the country.

The attacks on Belo follow an interview published in the German news magazine Der Spiegel in which he was reported as saying Indonesian troops had trampled on East Timor's independence "and treated us like dogs".
Belo, who flew to Jakarta on Monday for an annual meeting of Catholic bishops, has declined to comment until he sees the full text of the interview.
"We are protesting against the criticism of Bishop Belo," one demonstrator was quoted by an eyewitness as saying.

A statement given by students to the official National Commission on Human Rights at a heated meeting in Dili on Tuesday said the protests in Jakarta were an attempt to provoke antagonism between East Timorese and other Indonesians.
The statement said attacks on Belo were deliberately designed to discredit him and promote instability in East Timor.
"An attitude that is anti Bishop Belo is also against the East Timor community," it said.
Belo was jointly awarded the 1996 Nobel Peace Prize with self-exiled East Timorese-born independence activist Jose Ramos-Horta last month.

The protests came a day after the fifth anniversary of the shooting by troops of at least 50 demonstrators on their way to the Santa Cruz cemetery in Dili following the funeral of an anti-Indonesian activist killed two weeks earlier.
Indonesian troops invaded the former Portuguese colony in December 1975 and Jakarta declared it Indonesia's 27th province the following July in a move not recognised by the United Nations.
Four East Timorese men entered the Spanish embassy in Jakarta on Tuesday seeking political asylum.
The International Committee of the Red Cross's local delegation chief Henri Fournier said preparations were still being made, "but most probably they will be able to leave tonight".
They were expected to go to Portugal, which has granted refuge to 89 other East Timorese since September last year.
